entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very important, exciting or successful, as in *This is huge.*
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, sports talk and business chat about news that matters a lot: *Congrats on the promotion, that's huge!* It also describes a very popular person or thing (*The band is huge in Japan*). The literal sense *very large* is standard English; context shows which one is meant.
examples: You got the job offer? That's **huge**, congratulations!
Getting our biggest client to renew was **huge** for the company this year.
That band was **huge** in the nineties; everyone I knew had their album.

drill.sentence: Winning tonight would be {{huge}} for the team; they haven't made the playoffs in ten years.
drill.hint: very important (one word, casual; not *big* or *massive*)

entries.related: *a big deal* — important, casual; *massive* — similar, a little stronger; *big* in *big news* — neutral.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To go and see a movie, usually as a relaxed, casual plan; *catch a show* or *catch a game* works the same way.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and texts for all ages: *Want to catch a movie tonight?* It suggests an easy, unplanned outing and works with other events too: *catch a show*, *catch a game*, *catch a band*. *Catch* also means *see or hear something in time*, as in *Did you catch the news?*
entries.pattern: catch a movie / a show / a game
examples: We have a couple of hours before dinner; want to **catch a movie**?
When my parents visited New York, we **caught a Broadway show** on their last night.
A few of us are going to **catch the Cubs game** at a bar downtown if you want to come.

drill.sentence: It's raining too hard to go hiking, so let's {{catch a movie}} at the theater downtown instead.
drill.hint: go and see a film, casually (the verb is not *see* or *watch*)

entries.related: *go to the movies* — neutral; *see a show* — neutral; *catch up on a show* — watch episodes you missed.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To spread very fast and widely on the internet, as huge numbers of people share a video, post or photo.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in speech, news and marketing: *Her video went viral overnight.* It is informal but so common that journalists use it freely. The subject is usually a video, post, photo or song, sometimes the person who posted it; the adjective is *viral* (*a viral video*).
examples: My cousin's video of her cat playing the piano **went viral**, and now it has ten million views.
A bakery's funny sign **went viral**, and people drove in from three states to see it.
Our company's ad was supposed to **go viral**, but only about two hundred people watched it.

drill.sentence: The clip of the dog stealing the ball at the soccer game {{went viral}} within hours.
drill.hint: spread fast online (two words; not *blew up*)

entries.related: *blow up* — slang, suddenly become very popular online; *be trending* — be among the most discussed topics; *a viral video* — the adjective.

entries.term: have the guts to do something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have the courage to do something difficult, risky or unpleasant.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, often in the negative or as admiration: *I didn't have the guts to tell her.* *Guts* is always plural in this sense. *It takes guts to* + verb is another common pattern, and *gutsy* is the adjective.
entries.pattern: have the guts to + verb; it takes guts to + verb
examples: I wanted to ask for a raise, but I didn't **have the guts to** do it.
It **takes guts** to quit a stable job and open your own restaurant.
He finally **had the guts to** call his dad and apologize after five years.

drill.sentence: Nobody else would say it, but Rachel {{had the guts to}} stand up at the town meeting and complain about the noise.
drill.hint: found enough courage to (four words; not *had the nerve to* or *had the courage to*)

entries.related: *have the nerve to* — similar, but often critical (= be rude enough to); *gutsy* — brave, informal; *chicken out* — lose your courage and not do it.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To study a lot in a short time just before an exam.
entries.usage: Common among students, and among adults remembering school: *I crammed all night.* It is often slightly critical, suggesting you left everything to the last minute and won't remember it for long. Typical patterns are *cram for* + exam and *a cram session*.
examples: I didn't open the textbook all semester, so I had to **cram** the night before the final.
My son is **cramming for** his driving test with an app on his phone.
Instead of **cramming**, try studying a little every day; you'll remember much more.

drill.sentence: Jake stayed up until three a.m. {{cramming}} for his chemistry test and then fell asleep in class.
drill.hint: studying hard at the last minute (not *studying* or *reviewing*)

entries.related: *pull an all-nighter* — stay up all night, often to study; *study up on something* — learn about it before an event; *review* — go over material calmly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An expert, or someone very skilled at something, whether or not they do it as a job.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, often as praise for someone who handles something smoothly: *You're a pro at this!* *Like a pro* means very skillfully (*She parallel parks like a pro*). It is short for *professional*, so in sports *a pro* is also a paid player.
examples: Watch Dave flip those pancakes; he's **a pro** at this.
After two weeks of practice, my daughter was riding her bike **like a pro**.
Let the movers do it; they're **pros**, and they'll have the piano downstairs in ten minutes.

drill.sentence: Ask Carmen to help you set up the tent; she's been camping for years and she's {{a pro}}.
drill.hint: someone very skilled, short for a longer job word (not *an expert*)

entries.related: *an expert* — neutral; *a natural* — someone who is good at something without much training; *a rookie* — a beginner.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To invite someone to go on a date with you.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in speech and writing: *He finally asked her out.* A pronoun goes between *ask* and *out*, and you can add *on a date* or *to dinner*. Without *out*, *ask someone* just means to ask them a question, so *out* is essential.
entries.pattern: ask someone out (on a date / to dinner)
examples: Sam finally **asked her out** after weeks of chatting at the dog park.
I'm too nervous to **ask him out**, so I'm hoping he'll ask me first.
My roommate **got asked out** twice at the same wedding.

drill.sentence: If you like her that much, just {{ask her out}}! The worst she can say is no.
drill.hint: invite her on a date (three words; not *take her out*)

entries.related: *go out with someone* — date someone; *take someone out* — go somewhere with someone and usually pay; *a date* — a romantic meeting.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be dating someone, usually in an early or not yet serious relationship.
entries.usage: Common in conversation for all ages: *Are you seeing anyone?* In this sense it is usually progressive, and it sounds less serious than *be in a relationship*. It is a polite, gentle way to ask about someone's love life.
examples: My sister's been **seeing** a guy from her running club, but it's still pretty new.
"Are you **seeing** anyone?" "Not right now; I'm focusing on work."
They were **seeing** each other for a few months before they told their friends.

drill.sentence: Is Daniel single, or is he {{seeing}} someone? He's been really happy lately.
drill.hint: going out with, not yet seriously (one word, -ing form; not *dating*)

entries.related: *date someone* — similar, a bit more direct; *go out with someone* — be in a relationship; *be in a relationship* — more serious.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To like each other and get along well right away, as if you had known each other for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech about friendships, romance and teams: *We just clicked.* The patterns are *click with someone* or *A and B clicked*, often with *right away*, *instantly* or *just*. A different informal sense is *suddenly become clear* (*Then it clicked*).
entries.pattern: click with someone; A and B clicked
examples: I met my best friend on the first day of college, and we **clicked** right away.
She went on a few dates with him, but they never really **clicked**.
Our daughter **clicked with** the girl next door the day we moved in, and now they're inseparable.

drill.sentence: We met at a friend's wedding, started talking about old movies and just {{clicked}}.
drill.hint: got along instantly (one word; not *connected*, *bonded* or *hit it off*)

entries.related: *hit it off* — the same meaning, very common; *get along* — have a friendly relationship; *have chemistry* — feel a natural connection, often romantic.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have known each other for a long time, often since childhood or school.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, often to explain a close or trusting relationship: *Mike and I go way back.* The subject is usually plural (*we*, *A and B*), or you say *go way back with someone*. It suggests a long, warm friendship and is fine when introducing people at work.
examples: "How do you know Jake?" "Oh, we **go way back**; we played Little League together."
The owner gave us a free dessert because he and my dad **go way back**.
Our families **go way back**; our dads opened a hardware store together in the eighties.

drill.sentence: Tom and I {{go way back}}; we were roommates in college almost twenty years ago.
drill.hint: have been friends for many years (three words)

entries.related: *go back a long way* — the same, more common in British English; *an old friend* — neutral; *know someone from way back* — similar idea.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone or something worth keeping, especially a partner who is good enough for a long-term relationship.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech as warm praise of a new partner (*He's a keeper*), often from friends or family who have just met them. It is also used about a recipe, a car or anything worth holding on to. In sports, *keeper* is short for *goalkeeper*, a separate sense.
examples: He cooked dinner, did the dishes and remembered my mom's birthday; he's **a keeper**.
This lasagna recipe is **a keeper**; I'm making it again next week.
My parents met my girlfriend once and told me she's **a keeper**.

drill.sentence: She's kind, funny and gets along with your whole family; that one's {{a keeper}}.
drill.hint: worth holding on to for good (two words; not *a catch* or *a gem*)

entries.related: *a catch* — an attractive partner that many people would want; *the one* — the person you'll marry; *a gem* — a very good person or thing.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: My home, whether it's a house, an apartment or a room, as in *Let's go back to my place.*
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech: *Come over to my place*, *dinner at her place*. It doesn't say what kind of home it is, so it's convenient when *apartment* or *house* doesn't matter. *Your place or mine?* can suggest romance, so context matters.
examples: Do you want to watch the game at **my place**? I have a big TV and plenty of snacks.
We're having a small birthday dinner at **Jenna's place** on Saturday.
After the concert, everyone went back to **his place** and stayed up until four.

drill.sentence: The bars are all packed, so let's just go back to {{my place}} and order a pizza.
drill.hint: where I live (two words; not *my apartment* or *my house*)

entries.related: *my apartment* / *my house* — more specific; *come over* — visit someone's home; *crash at someone's place* — sleep there for a night.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go to a party or event without being invited.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, often in a funny story: *We crashed a wedding.* The person is *a party crasher* or *a wedding crasher*. It can be harmless fun or rude, depending on the event and the host.
entries.pattern: crash a party / a wedding / an event
examples: Some guys from another school **crashed the party**, and the host had to ask them to leave.
My little brother **crashed** my sleepover and ate all our popcorn.
Two strangers **crashed** my cousin's wedding and somehow ended up giving a toast.

drill.sentence: Nobody invited Kevin, but he {{crashed the party}} anyway and ate half the cake.
drill.hint: showed up at the celebration without an invitation (three words)

entries.related: *a gatecrasher* — a similar noun, more British; *show up uninvited* — neutral; *crash at someone's place* — sleep there, a different meaning.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: Said when something is completely obvious, often to tease someone who has just asked or said something obvious.
entries.usage: Slang, common among teenagers and younger adults and used jokingly by older people too. Aimed at someone else it mocks them a little, so it's rude unless you're teasing a friend. Said about yourself after a silly mistake (*Oh, duh, it's Tuesday*), it is friendly and self-mocking.
examples: "Is it cold outside?" "**Duh**, it's January in Minnesota."
I spent ten minutes looking for my glasses, and they were on my head. **Duh**.
"Wait, you need a ticket to get in?" "Well, **duh**. It's a concert."

drill.sentence: "Should I bring a towel to the beach?" "{{Duh}}! You're going swimming, aren't you?"
drill.hint: of course, that's obvious (teasing slang, one syllable; not *obviously*)

entries.related: *obviously* — neutral, can still sound rude; *no kidding* — sarcastic agreement; *of course* — polite.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A teasing reply meaning *that won't happen, however much you want it*.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, usually between friends or siblings and with a playful tone. It answers someone's hopeful or boastful claim (*I'm going to beat you!* — *You wish!*). With strangers or in a serious conversation it sounds dismissive.
examples: "I'm going to beat you at chess this time." "**You wish**!"
"Admit it, you think I'm the funniest person you know." "Ha, **you wish**."
My brother asked if he could have my car when I move away, and I just said, "**You wish**."

drill.sentence: "I'm going to win our family's fantasy football league this year." "{{You wish}}! You haven't won a single game."
drill.hint: that's never going to happen, said teasingly (two words; not *no way* or *dream on*)

entries.related: *dream on* — similar, a bit stronger; *in your dreams* — the same idea; *I wish* — a different reply: *I'd like that too, but it's unlikely*.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly reaction to surprising news, meaning *I don't believe you!* or *No way!*
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, said with a smile and sometimes a playful push; in fast speech it sounds like *get outta here*. Only the tone separates it from the literal, angry order to leave the room. Fine among friends and friendly coworkers.
examples: "I'm getting married!" "**Get out of here!** When did that happen?"
"I won two tickets to the World Series." "**Get out of here!** Are you serious?"
"My mom used to sing in a punk band." "**Get out of here**, really?"

drill.sentence: "Guess what? I got the apartment with the rooftop pool." "{{Get out of here}}! How much is the rent?"
drill.hint: I can't believe it, said happily (four words; not *no way* or *shut up*)

entries.related: *No way!* — very similar, very common; *Shut up!* — playful disbelief among younger friends; *You're kidding!* — neutral surprise.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual spoken form of *(I've) got you*: *I understand*; also *I caught you!* when you trick or catch someone.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and in quick chat messages at work: *Gotcha, I'll send it by noon.* As *I understand*, it is friendly and quick, but in a formal email write *Understood* or *Thanks, will do*. Said with a laugh after a trick or a prank, it means *I fooled you* or *I caught you*.
examples: "Park in the back; the front lot is for customers." "**Gotcha**, thanks."
**Gotcha**! I knew you were the one stealing my fries.
My son jumped out from behind the door, yelled "**Gotcha**!" and laughed when I screamed.

drill.sentence: "The spare key is under the flowerpot by the back door." "Oh, {{gotcha}}. Thanks!"
drill.hint: I understand, said fast and casually (one word; not *got it*)

entries.related: *got it* — the same meaning, slightly more neutral; *I see* — neutral; *gotcha journalism* — reporting that tries to catch people making mistakes.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said at the end of a short list to mean *and anything else you can think of*: all kinds of things.
entries.usage: Common in speech and casual writing, usually after two or three examples. It stresses how many different things there are, often with a bit of humor or exaggeration. It is informal but fine in relaxed talk at work or in a blog post.
examples: My father-in-law can fix anything: cars, clocks, dishwashers, **you name it**.
The thrift store sells old records, wedding dresses, garden tools, **you name it**.
"What kind of food do they have at the state fair?" "**You name it**; they even fry candy bars."

drill.sentence: The airport shop had magazines, phone chargers, neck pillows, {{you name it}}.
drill.hint: and anything else you can think of (three words; not *and so on*)

entries.related: *and so on* — neutral; *the works* — everything available (*a burger with the works*); *and whatnot* — casual, *and similar things*.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *No problem*: a reply to thanks or a request, or a comment that something was easy.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech among all ages, and a bit more relaxed than *no problem*. It answers thanks (*Thanks for the ride.* — *No sweat.*) or says a task is easy (*Fixing it was no sweat*). Fine with friends and coworkers, but not in a formal email.
examples: "Thanks for helping me move the couch." "**No sweat**, man."
"Can you grab my mail while I'm away?" "Sure, **no sweat**."
The first part of the test was **no sweat**, but the essay question was brutal.

drill.sentence: "Could you grab me a coffee on your way in?" "{{No sweat}}, I'm going there anyway."
drill.hint: it's easy, happy to (casual US, two words; not *no problem*, *no worries* or *sure thing*)

entries.related: *no problem* — the neutral version; *no worries* — similar, originally Australian; *a piece of cake* — something very easy.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To be great or excellent, as in *You rock!* or *This song rocks.*
entries.usage: Cheerful slang that sounds a bit dated to some young people, but *You rock!* is still a very common, warm way to thank someone, and fine with friendly coworkers. *This song rocks* praises music, food or an event. *Rock* + clothing (*She's rocking that hat*) means wearing it with confidence.
examples: You fixed my bike in ten minutes? **You rock**!
This new playlist **rocks**; I've had it on repeat all morning.
Mr. Davis **rocks**; he brings donuts to class every Friday.

drill.sentence: Thanks for lending me your tent for the weekend. You totally {{rock}}!
drill.hint: are great (slang verb; not *rule*)

entries.related: *rule* — similar slang (*You rule!*); *you're the best* — warm thanks, less slangy; *stink* — the informal opposite, be bad.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To be very bad, unfair or disappointing, as in *That stinks*; *stink at* something means to be very bad at it.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech among all ages, and mild enough for kids and coworkers. *That stinks* is a sympathetic reaction to someone's bad news, and *I stink at* + activity is a modest way to admit you're bad at something. It is a softer, more family-friendly word than *suck*.
examples: You have to work all weekend? That **stinks**.
I **stink** at bowling, but I go anyway because my friends are fun.
The new parking rules **stink**; now I have to pay just to park outside my own building.

drill.sentence: "I didn't get the internship." "Oh no, that really {{stinks}}. I'm sorry."
drill.hint: is really bad and disappointing (casual US verb; not *sucks*)

entries.related: *suck* — the same meaning, slangier and cruder; *That's a bummer* — milder; *be terrible at something* — the neutral version of *stink at*.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A confident reply meaning *I'm ready for the challenge; let's do it.*
entries.usage: Common in casual speech about sports, games and friendly competition, and often a little playful or showy. It answers a challenge or a threat (*We'll beat you next week* — *Bring it on!*). Said about a hard task, it shows determination rather than fear.
examples: "Our team is going to crush you in the trivia contest." "Oh yeah? **Bring it on**."
The forecast says two feet of snow tomorrow. **Bring it on**; I just bought a snowblower.
My sister challenged me to a pie-eating contest at the fair, and I said, "**Bring it on**!"

drill.sentence: "Think you can beat me at ping-pong?" "{{Bring it on}}! I've been practicing all summer."
drill.hint: I accept your challenge (three words; not *you're on* or *game on*)

entries.related: *you're on* — I accept your bet or challenge; *game on* — the competition starts now; *let's do this* — ready to start.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said when an annoying or unpleasant thing that has happened before starts happening again.
entries.usage: Common in speech for all ages, said with a sigh or an eye roll about arguments, delays, bad habits or familiar problems. It's usually a comment to yourself or a friend, and it can sound rude if said directly to the person causing the problem. The tone is tired and resigned, sometimes humorous.
examples: The car's making that weird noise. **Here we go again**; it's going back to the mechanic.
Dad started telling his story about the fish he almost caught, and Mom whispered, "**Here we go again**."
Every spring the city digs up our street for new pipes, and every spring we say, "**Here we go again**."

drill.sentence: My roommates just started arguing about the dishes again. Oh great, {{here we go again}}.
drill.hint: the same old annoying thing is starting once more (four words; not *story of my life*)

entries.related: *not again* — shorter, similar; *story of my life* — this bad luck always happens to me; *déjà vu* — the feeling that you've lived a moment before.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A humorous complaint meaning *this kind of bad luck always happens to me*.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and texts for all ages, usually right after a small disappointment, said with a sigh or a laugh. It is self-pitying in a joking way, so it suits small problems, not serious ones. It usually stands alone, often without *the*: *Story of my life.*
examples: The bus pulled away just as I got to the stop. **Story of my life**.
"They sold the last slice of cheesecake right before you ordered?" "Yep, **story of my life**."
Every time I wash my car, it rains the next day; it's the **story of my life**.

drill.sentence: I finally found jeans I like, and of course they don't have my size. {{Story of my life}}.
drill.hint: this kind of bad luck always happens to me (four words; not *just my luck*)

entries.related: *here we go again* — the same annoying thing is starting again; *just my luck* — similar, about bad luck; *figures* — casual, *that's what I expected*.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *Stop doing that*, said to someone whose behavior is annoying you.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, especially from parents to kids, between siblings, or between friends who are teasing. It is direct and a little irritated but not rude among people who know each other well; with strangers it sounds bossy. *Cut that out* means the same.
examples: **Cut it out**, you two! Stop kicking each other in the back seat.
Every time I mention Jake, you start grinning. **Cut it out**; we're just friends.
My brother kept poking me during dinner until Mom told him to **cut it out**.

drill.sentence: Will you {{cut it out}}? I'm trying to sleep and you keep tapping your pen.
drill.hint: stop doing that, said irritably (three words; not *knock it off*, *quit it* or *stop it*)

entries.related: *knock it off* — the same, a bit stronger; *quit it* — the same, very casual; *cut something out* — remove it, or stop eating it (*cut out sugar*).

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *Stop talking about it; let it go*: said when you want a topic or an argument to end.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and usually a little irritated: *Can we just drop it?* It's used when a topic is painful, embarrassing or causing an argument, and *Just drop it* sounds sharper. To a dog, *Drop it!* is the command to let go of something in its mouth.
examples: I said I'm sorry about the car. Can we please just **drop it**?
Mom started asking about my breakup, saw my face and **dropped it**.
It's not worth fighting about; let's **drop it** and enjoy dinner.

drill.sentence: "But why did you quit your job?" "I don't want to talk about it. Please, just {{drop it}}."
drill.hint: stop asking about this topic (two words; not *leave it* or *forget it*)

entries.related: *let it go* — stop worrying or arguing about it; *forget it* — it doesn't matter; *change the subject* — start talking about something else.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *Say it, stop hesitating*: said to someone who is slow to say what they want to say.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, often impatient but also used kindly to push a nervous friend: *Come on, spit it out.* Because it is so direct, it can sound rude to a coworker or a stranger. It often comes with *just* or *come on*.
examples: You've been trying to tell me something all night. **Spit it out**.
Come on, just **spit it out**; what did the doctor say?
He stood there mumbling for a minute until his sister said, "**Spit it out**, Ben!"

drill.sentence: "So, um, there's something I need to tell you about your car." "Okay, {{spit it out}}. What happened?"
drill.hint: say it now, stop hesitating (three words; not *out with it*)

entries.related: *out with it* — the same, a bit old-fashioned; *get to the point* — stop giving unnecessary details; *beat around the bush* — avoid saying something directly.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *Control your emotions and calm down*; often said to someone who is overreacting.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, usually blunt and a little impatient. Said to someone who is really upset it can sound harsh, so it's mostly used with friends or about yourself (*I need to get a grip*). *Get a grip on something* means gain control of a situation.
examples: It's only a spider, Kevin. **Get a grip**.
I cried at a car commercial yesterday. I really need to **get a grip**.
Okay, **get a grip**; it's one bad grade, not the end of the world.

drill.sentence: You're yelling because they forgot the ketchup? {{Get a grip}}; it's not a big deal.
drill.hint: control yourself, stop overreacting (three words; not *calm down*, *chill out* or *relax*)

entries.related: *calm down* — neutral; *pull yourself together* — similar, a bit more sympathetic; *lose it* — lose control of your emotions.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *Be realistic; stop believing something unlikely*: said to someone with a silly hope or idea.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech; it is blunt and a little mocking, so use it only with people you know well. It answers unrealistic plans, excuses or claims, often right after you repeat them as a question. It is stronger than *be realistic* and close to *don't be ridiculous*.
examples: You think you'll finish the whole basement this weekend? **Get real**.
"Maybe the airline will give us a full refund." "**Get real**; they won't even answer the phone."
My brother says he'll be a millionaire by thirty, and I keep telling him to **get real**.

drill.sentence: "I'll just learn Japanese in a month before our trip." "Oh, {{get real}}. It takes years."
drill.hint: be realistic, stop dreaming (two words; not *come on* or *dream on*)

entries.related: *be realistic* — neutral; *dream on* — mocking, *that will never happen*; *keep it real* — slang, be honest and authentic, a different meaning.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: *It isn't too much to ask*: said to push someone to do something small that they don't want to do.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, especially from parents, partners and friends, and often half-joking. It can sound pushy or annoyed, so be careful with it. Typical patterns are *It won't kill you to* + verb and the more sarcastic question *Would it kill you to* + verb?
entries.pattern: It won't kill you (to + verb); Would it kill you to + verb?
examples: Just call your aunt on her birthday; **it won't kill you**.
**It won't kill you to** wear a tie for one evening.
**Would it kill you to** text me when you're going to be late?

drill.sentence: I know you hate hiking, but come with us this once; {{it won't kill you}}.
drill.hint: it's not too much to ask (four words; a stronger verb than *hurt*)

entries.related: *it won't hurt to* + verb — milder, means it's a good idea; *humor me* — do it just to please me; *it's the least you can do* — you owe it.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To scold someone angrily and at length, usually for a mistake.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, mostly about bosses, coaches, teachers and parents: *My boss chewed me out.* A pronoun goes between *chew* and *out*, and the passive with *get* is very common (*I got chewed out*). *For* + noun or -ing gives the reason.
entries.pattern: chew someone out (for + -ing); get chewed out
examples: My manager **chewed me out** in front of the whole team for missing the deadline.
The coach **chewed out** the players at halftime, and they came back and won.
I **got chewed out** by my mom for coming home at two in the morning.

drill.sentence: Dad {{chewed us out}} for leaving the back door open all night.
drill.hint: criticized us angrily and at length (US; not *yelled at us* or *told us off*)

entries.related: *yell at someone* — shout angrily, more general; *tell someone off* — scold, also common in British English; *give someone an earful* — complain angrily to them.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Extremely; used right before an adjective, as in *crazy busy* or *crazy expensive*.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech among younger and middle-aged adults: *Work has been crazy busy.* It goes before adjectives (*crazy good*, *crazy expensive*) and is too casual for formal writing. *Crazy* as an adjective (*That's crazy*) is a different use.
examples: Work has been **crazy** busy this month, so I haven't had time to call anyone.
Houses in this town are **crazy** expensive now; my parents couldn't afford theirs today.
The tacos at that food truck are **crazy** good; get the fish ones.

drill.sentence: Sorry I haven't texted back; things at the restaurant have been {{crazy}} busy since the holidays.
drill.hint: extremely; normally an adjective meaning *mad* (not *so*, *super*, *really* or *insanely*)

entries.related: *super* — a casual intensifier, softer; *insanely* — even stronger; *like crazy* — very much or very fast, after a verb.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Very much, very fast or very hard; it comes after a verb, as in *work like crazy*.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages: *It's been raining like crazy.* It goes at the end of a clause, after the verb it describes, and shows great intensity or speed. *Like mad* means the same and is also common in British English.
examples: My phone's been buzzing **like crazy** since I posted our engagement photos.
It snowed **like crazy** last night, and the schools are closed today.
The puppy ran around the yard **like crazy** for ten minutes and then fell asleep.

drill.sentence: I miss you {{like crazy}}; I can't wait until you're back from Spain.
drill.hint: very, very much (two words, after the verb; not *so much*, *a lot* or the version ending in *mad*)

entries.related: *like mad* — the same; *like there's no tomorrow* — without any limit (*spending like there's no tomorrow*); *crazy* + adjective — extremely (*crazy busy*).

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Completely or exactly, before certain adjectives and words: *dead serious*, *dead tired*, *dead wrong*.
entries.usage: Common in speech for all ages, but in American English only in fixed combinations: *dead serious*, *dead tired*, *dead wrong*, *dead center*, *dead set on* (= determined to). In British English *dead* is also a general intensifier (*dead easy*, *dead good*), which sounds British to Americans.
examples: I'm not joking; I'm **dead serious** about moving to Alaska.
By the end of moving day we were **dead tired**, so we slept on a mattress on the floor.
The picture has to hang **dead center** over the couch, or my wife will notice.

drill.sentence: Everyone in town thought the old man was broke, but they were {{dead}} wrong; he left the library two million dollars.
drill.hint: 100 percent (one short informal word; not *totally*, *so* or *way*)

entries.related: *totally* / *completely* — neutral; *dead set on something* — completely determined to do it; *dead* + adjective in British English (*dead easy*) — very.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Extremely bored; *scared to death* and *worried to death* use the same exaggeration.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages as an exaggeration: *I was bored to death.* The pattern *adjective + to death* works only with a few feelings: *scared to death*, *worried to death*, *sick to death of* (= completely fed up with). *Bored to tears* means the same as *bored to death*.
examples: The lecture was two hours of slides with tiny text, and I was **bored to death**.
My kids get **bored to death** on long car rides unless they have something to watch.
I was **scared to death** when the plane dropped suddenly over the mountains.

drill.sentence: Three hours of my uncle's vacation photos? I was {{bored to death}}.
drill.hint: so uninterested I could die (three words; not the version that ends in *tears*)

entries.related: *bored to tears* — the same; *sick to death of something* — completely fed up with it; *scared stiff* — very frightened.

entries.label: suffix
entries.meaning: A suffix meaning *approximately* or *somewhat*: *seven-ish* (about seven o'clock), *tired-ish* (a bit tired).
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts, especially with times and ages (*sevenish*, *fortyish*), colors and adjectives (*greenish*, *tallish*). In speech it can even stand alone as a hedge: *Are you ready?* — *Ish.* Spelling varies: *sevenish* or *seven-ish*.
examples: Let's meet at the park around **six-ish**; I'll text you if I'm running late.
Her new boyfriend is **fortyish**, with gray hair and a really loud laugh.
"Did you finish the report?" "**Ish**. I still need to add the charts."

drill.sentence: Dinner's at my place on Sunday; come over at seven-{{ish}} and bring a salad if you can.
drill.hint: a casual suffix meaning *roughly*

entries.related: *about* / *around* — neutral, before the number; *give or take* — after a number; *kind of* — *somewhat*, before an adjective.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: In slang: very impressive, great or extreme, as in *an epic party*; *an epic fail* is a huge, often funny failure.
entries.usage: Slang popular with younger people and online; adults use it too, often jokingly. *Epic* + noun (*an epic road trip*, *an epic fail*) is the main pattern, and *That was epic!* is a reaction. The standard sense, *a long story or film about heroic events*, is neutral.
examples: We drove from Boston to San Diego in five days; it was an **epic** road trip.
His attempt to fix the sink ended with water all over the kitchen, an **epic** fail.
The snowball fight on our street last night was **epic**; even the parents joined in.

drill.sentence: My brother tried to do a backflip off the dock and landed flat on his stomach. {{Epic}} fail.
drill.hint: the slang adjective in the set phrase for a huge, funny failure (not *total*, *major* or *massive*)

entries.related: *legendary* — slang, so great people will talk about it; *awesome* — great, more common; *a fail* — slang noun, a failure.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: *Great!*: a happy reaction to good news or a good plan; before a noun it means *excellent*, as in *a sweet deal*.
entries.usage: Slang, common among younger Americans and used by many adults too as a quick, happy reaction: *Oh, sweet!* Before a noun it means *excellent* (*a sweet ride*, *a sweet deal*). Keep it out of work emails; the normal senses, *tasting of sugar* and *kind*, are standard English.
examples: "I got us tickets for Saturday." "**Sweet**! What time does it start?"
My neighbor got a **sweet** deal on a used truck: low miles and half the usual price.
Your new apartment has a **sweet** view of the river.

drill.sentence: "The boss said we can leave at three today." "{{Sweet}}! I'll beat the traffic for once."
drill.hint: a happy one-word slang reaction (not *nice*, *cool*, *awesome*, *great* or *perfect*)

entries.related: *awesome* — great, very common; *nice* — milder approval; *sweet* about a person — kind and gentle, standard English.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Nice, clever or interesting, as in *That's neat.*
entries.usage: Common in American speech among all ages, but it sounds mild and a little old-fashioned or wholesome, so younger people often prefer *cool*. It's used for clever ideas, gadgets and small surprises (*What a neat trick*). The standard senses, *tidy* and *(of a drink) with no ice or water*, are used in both countries.
examples: The museum has a **neat** exhibit where you can build your own bridge out of blocks.
You can fold this bike up and carry it on the train? That's pretty **neat**.
The bartender showed us a **neat** trick with a coin and a napkin.

drill.sentence: "This app tells you which plants are poisonous to your cat." "Oh, that's {{neat}}!"
drill.hint: interesting in a pleasing way; mild and a bit old-fashioned (not *cool*, *nice*, *clever* or *handy*)

entries.related: *cool* — similar, more common among younger people; *nifty* — clever and useful, a bit old-fashioned; *neat* = *tidy* — the standard sense.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Stylish and elegant, showing good taste; about behavior, it means dignified and gracious.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech about places, clothes and behavior: *a classy restaurant*, *a classy move*. About behavior it praises grace or good manners, especially in a difficult moment. It is also often used sarcastically about rude behavior (*Wow, classy*).
examples: For our anniversary we went to a **classy** restaurant with white tablecloths and live jazz.
She didn't say anything bad about her ex in the interview; that was really **classy**.
He burped loudly at the dinner table. Wow, very **classy**.

drill.sentence: Even after losing the final, she congratulated the winner with a big smile; that was really {{classy}}.
drill.hint: showing grace and good manners (informal; not *gracious*, *mature* or *nice*)

entries.related: *elegant* — neutral; *fancy* — expensive-looking, not always tasteful; *tacky* — the opposite, cheap and in bad taste.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very bad, of poor quality, or unpleasant; *feel lousy* means feel ill or unhappy.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages: *lousy weather*, *a lousy job*, *lousy service*. *Feel lousy* means you feel sick or miserable. *A lousy* + small amount (*a lousy five dollars*) complains that the amount is far too small.
examples: The food was great, but the service was **lousy**; we waited forty minutes for our drinks.
I've got a cold and I feel **lousy**, so I'm staying home today.
He worked overtime all week and got a **lousy** twenty-dollar gift card as thanks.

drill.sentence: The weather was {{lousy}} the whole week we were at the beach, so we played board games inside.
drill.hint: really poor and unpleasant (casual; not *awful*, *terrible*, *rotten* or *crummy*)

entries.related: *crummy* — similar, a bit milder; *awful* — neutral, stronger; *rotten* — informal, very bad.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Suspicious; seeming dishonest, wrong or not quite true.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and in journalism: *There's something fishy going on.* Typical patterns are *something fishy*, *sound fishy* and *smell fishy*. It is milder than an accusation: it says you have doubts, not proof.
examples: A stranger offered to buy my car for twice its value. Something about it seemed **fishy**.
His story about losing his wallet again sounded a little **fishy** to me.
The auditors found some **fishy** payments to a company nobody had heard of.

drill.sentence: The "bank" asked for my password in an email, which seemed {{fishy}}, so I called them instead.
drill.hint: making you think someone is lying or cheating (informal; not *suspicious*, *sketchy*, *shady* or *off*)

entries.related: *sketchy* — suspicious or unsafe, very common in the US; *shady* — dishonest; *smell a rat* — suspect that something is wrong.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Crazy or foolish; *go nuts* means become very excited or very angry.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages and milder than *crazy*; *You're nuts!* is often friendly teasing. *Go nuts* can be happy (*The crowd went nuts*) or angry (*Dad went nuts when he saw the bill*). *Be nuts about* someone or something means to love them.
entries.pattern: be nuts; go nuts; be nuts about something
examples: You're going to run a marathon with no training? You're **nuts**.
When the band came back for an encore, the crowd **went nuts**.
Mom will **go nuts** if she finds out we broke her favorite vase.

drill.sentence: My sister drove six hours just to buy a cake from her favorite bakery; she's completely {{nuts}}.
drill.hint: foolishly extreme, said lightly (one word; not *crazy*, *insane* or *bonkers*)

entries.related: *crazy* — similar, more common; *bonkers* — playful, more British; *be nuts about something* — love it.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Knowing nothing about something, or not understanding a situation at all.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, often about yourself: *I'm totally clueless about cars.* The patterns are *clueless about* + noun, or the word alone for someone who doesn't notice what is happening (*He's so clueless*). Said about someone else, it can sound unkind.
examples: I'm completely **clueless** about wine, so I just pick whatever bottle has the nicest label.
Everyone knew she liked him except him; he was totally **clueless**.
When my parents tried to set up the new TV, they were **clueless**, so they called me.

drill.sentence: I'm {{clueless}} about taxes, so I pay a guy to do mine every year.
drill.hint: with no idea at all (one word; not *lost* or *hopeless*)

entries.related: *have no idea* — neutral; *out of the loop* — not told about something; *oblivious* — not noticing, more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Fully focused and performing very well, so that everything seems easy.
entries.usage: Common in sports, gaming and work talk: *She was in the zone.* It describes a short period of deep focus during a game, a workout or creative work, when people don't want to be interrupted. *Get in the zone* means reach that state.
examples: Our goalie was **in the zone** last night; he stopped thirty-two shots.
Don't talk to me while I'm painting; I'm finally **in the zone**.
I put on my headphones, made coffee and got **in the zone** for three hours of writing.

drill.sentence: She made ten free throws in a row; she was totally {{in the zone}}.
drill.hint: completely focused and playing perfectly (three words; not *on fire* or *on a roll*)

entries.related: *on fire* — playing extremely well, often in sports; *on a roll* — having a series of successes; *in a flow state* — a psychology term for the same experience.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something very easy to do.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and also in ads: *Setup is a breeze.* It usually follows *be* or *make it* (*The new app makes it a breeze*). The verb *breeze through* something means to do it or pass it very easily.
examples: The bookcase came with clear instructions, so putting it together was **a breeze**.
With the new dishwasher, cleaning up after dinner is **a breeze**.
She **breezed through** her nursing exams and got a job right away.

drill.sentence: Don't worry about the hike; it's mostly flat and shady, so it's {{a breeze}}.
drill.hint: something that takes almost no effort (two words, a noun; not *a snap* or *a cinch*)

entries.related: *a piece of cake* — the same, very common; *a cinch* — very easy, also informal; *no sweat* — no problem, easy.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A complete failure, especially a movie, show, product or event that people expected to succeed.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and entertainment news: *The movie was a box-office flop.* It is used about public things like films, products, launches and parties, rarely about people. As a verb, *flop* means fail (*The show flopped*).
examples: The movie cost two hundred million dollars to make and was a total **flop**.
My surprise party was **a flop**; half the guests got the wrong date.
The new phone **flopped**, and the company stopped making it after six months.

drill.sentence: The restaurant's new menu was {{a flop}}; nobody ordered the kale pizza, so they dropped it after a month.
drill.hint: nobody liked it, so it failed completely (two words, a noun; not *a bust*, *a dud*, *a failure* or *a disaster*)

entries.related: *a bust* — a failure, also informal; *a dud* — something that doesn't work; *a hit* — the opposite, a big success.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A big success; something or someone very popular, such as a song, a movie, a dish or a guest.
entries.usage: Common in speech and entertainment news: *a hit song*, *a hit show*. In everyday life, *be a hit (with someone)* means people loved it: *The cake was a hit with the kids.* *A big hit* and *a huge hit* are common.
examples: Her first song was **a hit**, and it played on every radio station that summer.
Your potato salad was **a hit**; three people asked me for the recipe.
The petting zoo was **a huge hit** with the kids at the birthday party.

drill.sentence: The taco truck was {{a hit}} at the block party; the line never got shorter all afternoon.
drill.hint: loved by everyone (two words, a noun; not *a success* or *a smash*)

entries.related: *a smash (hit)* — a huge success, mainly songs and films; *a flop* — the opposite; *a crowd-pleaser* — something most people enjoy.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that isn't possible, allowed or going to happen.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and work chat: *The picnic's a no-go because of the rain.* It is used to cancel or reject a plan quickly, without much explanation. The opposite is *a go* (*The trip is a go*).
examples: We wanted to camp at the lake, but fires are banned this summer, so it's **a no-go**.
I asked if we could bring our dog to the wedding, and it's **a no-go**.
Dinner on Friday is **a no-go** for me; can we do Saturday instead?

drill.sentence: The beach trip is {{a no-go}}; there's a thunderstorm warning all weekend.
drill.hint: not going to happen (informal noun, hyphenated; not *off* or *canceled*)

entries.related: *a go* — approved, happening; *off* — canceled (*The trip is off*); *a deal-breaker* — something that makes you reject a whole offer.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something essential that you should have, do or see; also in compounds like *a must-see* or *a must-have*.
entries.usage: Common in speech, travel writing and ads: *Sunscreen is a must.* *For* + person shows who needs it (*a must for dog owners*). The compounds *a must-see*, *a must-have*, *a must-read* and *a must-try* are especially common in reviews.
examples: If you're hiking in July, a hat and lots of water are **a must**.
The night market is **a must-see** if you visit Taipei.
These rain boots are **a must-have** for anyone who walks a dog in Seattle.

drill.sentence: Good walking shoes are {{a must}} in Rome; you'll be on your feet all day.
drill.hint: something you really need (two words; not *essential* or *a necessity*)

entries.related: *essential* — neutral; *a necessity* — more formal; *a must-see* / *a must-read* — something you should see or read.
